title: Reimagining Legal Education Through Purpose-Built GPTs: A Suite of AI Tutors for Critical Thinking and Authentic Practice
author: Michael Guihot

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Guihot accepts the need to develop independent legal reasoning alongside AI competence and materially extends the cluster by proposing purpose-built AI tutors for repeated, practice-oriented exercises and individualised feedback. The contribution is a concrete instructional design, but its claimed benefits remain experience-based hypotheses rather than demonstrated learning outcomes.
qs: This paper introduces the Legal Practice Lab (LPL), a suite of purpose-built        GPTs designed to restore intellectual rigour while extending the reach of        individualised feedback.
I translated these observations into a set of design hypotheses.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts that exposure and one-off assessment do not establish durable legal competence, then materially extends the proposition by linking deliberate, repeated skills development to the prospective erosion of junior-lawyer apprenticeships and proposing AI-assisted cultivation of distinctively human capabilities. Its automation and teaching-effectiveness claims remain largely predictive rather than empirically demonstrated.
qs: Students were assessed on a single example of each and dispatched into the rest of their degree having notionally ‘learned’ these competencies.

The challenge is to identify which skills will remain distinctively human in legal practice and to develop those skills deliberately, rather than continuing to train graduates for tasks that will not exist in the form they once did.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Guihot accepts the cluster’s concern that automation of junior legal work threatens traditional skills development and materially extends it with a concrete educational response: purpose-built GPT tutors for scaffolded reasoning, drafting, feedback and practice simulation. The contribution remains a design proposal rather than evidence of improved outcomes.
qs: The work once performed by graduate lawyers is increasingly automated,        which creates both a challenge and an opportunity for legal educators; how to        develop the skills required of junior lawyers in legal practice, and to use AI itself to        do it.
Each tool targets a specific failure point in contemporary        legal pedagogy, from rehearsing partner-facing memoranda to simulating the        conditions of commercial litigation.

kp.k: Automation threatens the traditional junior-lawyer apprenticeship
kp.d: Guihot argues that AI increasingly automates document review, first-draft memoranda, research, contract mark-up, discovery and due diligence, removing work through which graduates traditionally developed professional competence. He describes the apprenticeship model as breaking down and recommends that law schools assume more responsibility for professional formation. These are the author's claims about the direction of change, rather than measured employment findings presented in the paper.
qs: The work once performed by graduate lawyers such as document review, first-draft memoranda, legal research, contract mark-up, discovery, and due diligence, is increasingly automated, and the trajectory is one way.

Law schools must do more of that work themselves, and they now have, for the first time, a tool capable of providing the kind of responsive, high-frequency practice that professional formation requires.

kp.k: Lawyer value shifts toward judgment and commercial understanding
kp.d: The author predicts that lawyers' value in the coming decades will depend on identifying the right questions, understanding clients' underlying concerns, weighing unlike risks and recognising commercially unhelpful legal answers. He recommends deliberately developing judgment, communication and strategic reasoning instead of preparing graduates only for increasingly automated tasks, warning that otherwise students may delegate thinking without being able to assess or defend the resulting advice.
qs: What it does not handle is judgment: the capacity to identify which question to ask before answering it, to read a client’s real concern that underlies their stated instructions, to weigh incommensurable risks, to know when a legally correct answer is commercially useless.
These skills and judgement will define a lawyer’s value in the coming decades, and they are precisely what legal education has struggled to teach at scale.

Without guided, high-frequency practice in exactly this kind of reasoning, students may instead learn to delegate thinking to machines that will produce outputs they cannot evaluate and advice they cannot defend.

kp.k: Purpose-built tutors address scarce feedback and reasoning practice
kp.d: The Legal Practice Lab comprises purpose-built ChatGPT applications intended to supplement broad curricula, large cohorts and limited contact hours with repeated, individualised reasoning and drafting practice. Guihot argues that occasional assessments do not adequately develop argument construction, counterargument handling or audience-sensitive writing. Flexible pacing and chunked tasks are intended to support students with differing developmental stages and study circumstances, including neurodivergent learners.
qs: Large cohorts and limited contact hours make high-frequency, personalised feedback difficult to sustain.
AI tutors can fill the gap by offering low- stakes practice at any hour, calibrated to different developmental stages, with difficulty escalating as competence grows.

Chunked tasks and individualised pacing support students who struggle because they are first-in-family, study part-time, balance full-time work with full-time study, or manage neurodivergent learning needs.

kp.k: Learning theories underpin iterative, authentic professional simulations
kp.d: Guihot grounds the suite in Herrington and Oliver's authentic learning framework, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Kolb's experiential learning cycle. These frameworks support realistic, ill-defined client tasks, incremental assistance beyond current student capability, and cycles of experience, reflection, conceptual refinement and experimentation. They provide the pedagogical rationale for the design rather than empirical evidence of the suite's effectiveness.
qs: The LPL embeds each of these elements, placing students inside realistic client matters where they must draw out the facts, commit to advice, and justify it to a professional audience.
The LPL tools function as that interlocutor, scaffolding reasoning incrementally until students can perform independently.
As Vygotsky would insist, the tools are at their most powerful when used alongside human teachers as guides rather than as substitutes for them.

kp.k: Development rests on teaching observations and iterative self-testing
kp.d: The methodology translates recurring teaching observations into design hypotheses: low-stakes reasoning practice should improve qualification of claims and counterarguments; scaffolded memoranda should improve structure; Socratic questioning should improve reasoning; and realistic simulations should improve engagement and interpersonal skills. Guihot reports iteratively self-testing instructions, difficulty, task chunking, feedback tone and integrity safeguards. The paper describes intended benefits, without reporting a student sample, comparative trial or measured learning outcomes.
qs: I developed these tools based on observations from my day-to-day teaching practice.
I translated these observations into a set of design hypotheses.

I developed the GPT instructions iteratively through self-testing, adjusting difficulty levels, reducing cognitive load through chunking and checklists, refining the tone of feedback, and strengthening integrity guardrails.

kp.k: Client simulations train commercially usable advice under uncertainty
kp.d: Red Fox simulates transactional problems presented by senior in-house counsel, requiring fact clarification, authority-based analysis and recommendations sensitive to risk, cost, timing and stakeholders. Greystone simulates Australian civil litigation through a demanding in-house counsel persona who deliberately supplies incomplete facts. Students must justify court selection, litigation strategy, evidentiary requirements and settlement options. These are simulated buyer-side interactions designed to rehearse professional judgment, not evidence of deployment in corporate legal departments.
qs: Students encounter the difference between a legally correct analysis and genuinely useful advice, and they learn to receive iterative, firm but fair feedback as a feature of professional work rather than a judgment on their ability.
She briefs students in a client-like way, providing enough facts to work with but deliberately leaving gaps like dates unconfirmed, contract terms ambiguous, or incomplete evidence.

Students must advise on legal issues with authority applied to facts, identify the appropriate court and justify it, develop a litigation strategy, assess evidentiary needs, and evaluate settlement options against commercial risk.

kp.k: Transactional simulations recreate contract and supervised deal workflows
kp.d: Greenfields requires students to elicit commercial instructions and construct contracts clause by clause, responding to simulated client objections and allocating risk. Martin & Abbott simulates an M&A law firm, placing junior learners under senior supervision through due diligence, risk allocation, transaction structuring and partner reporting. The Contract Drafting Mentor focuses on instructions, clause functions and trade-offs rather than on-demand boilerplate. Together these tools aim to rehearse parts of traditional transactional apprenticeship.
qs: Where the Contract Drafting Mentor teaches the craft of individual clauses, Greenfields teaches the whole task — turning a commercial conversation into a working legal document.
The work follows the arc of a real deal: due diligence, identifying and allocating risk, structuring the transaction, and reporting to the supervising partner.
It is the closest the suite comes to reproducing the supervised deal work through which junior corporate lawyers traditionally learned.
By posing one question at a time, highlighting trade-offs, and prompting revision, it shifts the student’s focus from copy-and-paste drafting to judgment, precision, and professional reasoning.

kp.k: Skills tutors make reasoning and professional writing explicit
kp.d: Socrates uses sequenced doctrinal questions, factual distinctions and corrections to rehearse legal reasoning. The Critical Thinking Tutor asks students to identify claims, support and counterpositions, qualifying conclusions under uncertainty. The Legal Memorandum Tutor structures partner-facing advice around issues, authority, factual application and practical recommendations, eliciting substance from students rather than supplying it. Claimed improvements are presented as the tools' pedagogical functions, not demonstrated comparative results.
qs: The tutor engages students with carefully sequenced questions anchored in Australian doctrine and method, probing text, purpose, precedent, and policy.
Working with short legal scenarios, students are asked what the claim is, what supports it, and what would count against it — and prompted to qualify conclusions where uncertainty warrants.
Rather than filling content, the tutor draws it from the student so that the student identifies what matters.

kp.k: Integrity safeguards require student contributions and source checking
kp.d: The tools are instructed not to ghostwrite assignments or provide complete answers, to require student-supplied ideas and sources, and to check claims against primary materials. Australian law and conventions provide jurisdictional grounding. Preserved interaction histories are intended to make reasoning and judgment calls visible to students and staff. These are design instructions and intended safeguards, qualified by the author's acknowledgement of language-model limitations.
qs: They are instructed to teach, not to ghostwrite, and to refuse to produce complete answers.
Each tool is instructed to avoid drafting assignments, to insist on student-supplied ideas and sources, and to verify claims against primary materials.
The preserved trail of interactions makes reasoning auditable, giving students and staff visibility into how answers were assembled and where judgment calls occurred.
The tools are instructed not to ghostwrite for students and to ensure, as best as a language model can, that responses are grounded in real sources.

kp.k: Human oversight and maintenance remain essential
kp.d: Guihot identifies hallucinations, edge cases, sparse doctrine, excessive scaffolding and feedback that rewards polished but substantively weak answers as risks. Updating prompts and content as law and curricula change creates an ongoing maintenance burden. He advocates augmentation rather than replacement of teachers: routine scaffolding and first-pass critique may free educators for strategic judgment and higher-order coaching, conditional on institutional resource allocation.
qs: Limitations include the brittleness characteristic of any language model: hallucinations, edge cases, and sparse doctrine each pose risks.
There is a real danger of over-scaffolding, of rewarding a structurally confident but substantively thin answer with carefully crafted feedback if the tools are used without critical oversight.
The need for ongoing prompt and content updates as law and curricula evolve adds a maintenance burden that is easy to underestimate.
None of these tools displaces teacher judgment.
Their function is to widen access to feedback and rehearsal so that teachers can concentrate on higher-order coaching if that is where institutional resources follow.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Guihot claims that AI is automating graduate-level legal tasks, weakening the traditional apprenticeship model and shifting more responsibility for professional formation to law schools.
pts.d: The author identifies document review, first-draft memoranda, legal research, contract mark-up, discovery and due diligence as increasingly automated. He presents this as an ongoing, one-directional change that removes formative junior-lawyer experience, rather than offering a numerical prediction of job losses. His proposed response is for law schools to use AI simulations to supply repeated, responsive practice.

pts.k: Guihot predicts that judgment, client understanding and commercially informed strategic reasoning will increasingly define lawyers' value as routine research and drafting are automated.
pts.d: He contrasts AI's claimed competence and low cost in routine tasks with human capacities to identify the right question, interpret clients' underlying concerns and weigh competing risks. He also warns that students who lack guided reasoning practice may delegate thinking to AI and become unable to evaluate or defend its output.

pts.k: Guihot proposes that purpose-built AI tutors can expand personalised feedback and develop practice-ready reasoning through repeated, realistic legal simulations.
pts.d: The Legal Practice Lab is a ChatGPT-based suite intended to complement teaching. Its simulated transactional clients, litigation client, contract-building client and M&A firm require students to elicit missing facts, apply authority, allocate risk, make strategic choices and revise advice. Other tutors scaffold contract drafting, Socratic dialogue, critical thinking and partner-facing memoranda. The claimed benefits are intended outcomes and design hypotheses, not reported measured learning gains. Guihot also claims that routine AI scaffolding can free teachers for higher-order coaching.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The paper offers professional and teaching experience, pedagogical theory and iterative self-testing; it does not report empirical outcome evaluations or quantified automation evidence.
pts.d: Guihot grounds the tool designs in ten years of legal practice, sixteen years as an academic and ten years of AI research, together with recurring observations of student difficulties. He invokes authentic learning, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Kolb's experiential learning cycle as theoretical support. A cognitive-apprenticeship reference accompanies the apprenticeship discussion, and Robb et al. (2025) is cited for changing legal practice and education. The paper supplies no adoption statistics, labour-market data, model benchmarks, controlled student trials or measured improvements. Tool descriptions and self-testing support the account of design, while anticipated educational effects are explicitly introduced as hypotheses.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Automation is described as already occurring; the shift in lawyers' value extends over coming decades, while tutoring benefits depend on pedagogical design, repeated use and human oversight.
pts.d: The draft supplies no dated forecast for disappearance of specific tasks or attainment of learning gains. The tutors are presented as available for trial, grounded in Australian law and intended to supplement rather than replace teachers. Integrity controls are instructions to avoid ghostwriting, require student contributions and check sources, not guarantees of reliable compliance. Guihot acknowledges hallucinations, edge cases, sparse doctrine, over-scaffolding and continuing maintenance needs. Reallocation of teachers' time to higher-order coaching is expressly conditional on institutional resources following that direction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are graduate lawyers, law students, legal educators and employers expecting practice-ready graduates, with particular intended benefits for students underserved by conventional teaching.
pts.d: Graduate lawyers face the loss or transformation of tasks that previously provided apprenticeship experience. Students are expected to gain AI literacy, defensible reasoning, professional drafting and commercial judgment; junior lawyers are also named users of the Contract Drafting Mentor. Law schools face greater professional-training responsibilities, and teachers may shift from routine feedback to advanced coaching while retaining oversight. Individual pacing is intended to support first-in-family, part-time, working and neurodivergent students. The simulated companies, in-house counsel and M&A firm are teaching environments, not evidence of deployment by actual legal-service buyers or providers. The paper does not forecast market shares, legal fees or access-to-justice outcomes.
